newsitem.title: GERMANY: New poll sees 82 pct of Germans for EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: New poll sees 82 pct of Germans for EMU delay.

text.p: Eighty-two percent of Germans, parting company with Chancellor Helmut Kohl, want European monetary union (EMU) to be delayed if member countries cannot meet the strict Maastricht criteria, according to a poll released on Sunday.

But they were evenly split at 47-47 percent on whether the single currency would be launched on time in 1999, said the IRNA poll for Focus magazine released in advance of Monday's publication. Six percent were undecided.

Only 12 percent wanted to stick to the schedule for introducing the euro currency whether or not the criteria -- especially the three percent deficit-to-GDP target -- were met, while another six percent were undecided.

A poll published on Thursday in the weekly Die Woche said 71 percent backed an EMU delay, something Kohl and a majority of German politicians oppose as a potentially serious setback for European economies.
"Helmut Kohl stands practically alone with his European policy," Focus wrote in a comment on the poll, which INRA conducted between June 3 and 5 with a sample of 1,006 people.

"Strict adherence to the (Maastricht) criteria is an illusion after the French election and the gold flop," it said, referring to the left-wing victory in France and Bonn's failed bid to have the Bundesbank revalue its gold and pay it a profit to finance its budget this year and qualify for meet EMU.
Focus said 81 percent opposed tax hikes to fill the budget gaps this year and only 17 percent were ready to accept them.
There was also strong feeling against other tax hikes -- 74 percent opposed a rise in VAT and 68 percent were against raising petrol taxes.

The only option those surveyed seemed to accept would be a continuation of the current 7.5 percent solidarity surcharge for east Germany. Fifty-three percent supported that option while 43 percent were opposed.

Kohl's Free Democrat (FDP) partners succeeded in having him agree to reduce that by two percentage points next year, but Finance Minister Theo Waigel is reported to be considering taking back that concession to be able to raise more funds.
Asked if Waigel should resign, 48 percent said yes and 43 percent said no and nine percent were undecided.
